title: Moving The Goalposts
description: Continuously changing the criteria for success or approval so the victim can never actually win.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Moving the goalposts is a rigged game of psychological keep-away. The manipulator demands you meet a specific standard to earn their love, approval, or peace. But the moment you meet that standard, they instantly shift the requirements further away, guaranteeing you remain in a permanent state of striving and failing.

sections.title: Manipulator's Objective
content: Keep the victim permanently off-balance and working for approval.
Ensure the manipulator never actually has to deliver the promised reward (affection, a commitment, an apology).
Destroy the victim's self-esteem by orchestrating constant failure.
Maintain total control of the power dynamic.

sections.title: How The Tactic Works
content: Step 1: The manipulator states a clear condition: 'If you just do X, I will be happy / commit / stop yelling.'
Step 2: The victim works exhausting amounts to achieve X.
Step 3: The victim presents X to the manipulator.
Step 4: The manipulator dismisses X as flawed or insufficient, and introduces requirement Y.

sections.title: Common Tactics Used
content: The 'It's About Time' shift: When you finally do what they asked, they complain that it took you too long, stealing the victory.
The Perfectionist shift: You cleaned the house like they asked, but they rage because you missed one specific corner.
The Milestone Delay: 'I will marry you when you get a better job.' (Gets job). 'Well, I want us to have more savings first.'
The Tone shift: 'You apologized, but your tone wasn't genuine enough.'

sections.title: Real Conversation Examples
content: Manipulator: 'I'd spend more time with you if you just showed interest in my hobbies.'
Victim (Learns manipulator's hobby and plans a weekend around it).
Manipulator: 'Wow, you're only doing this because I complained about it. It doesn't even count. It's so forced.'
Result: The victim puts in extreme effort and is punished even harder.

sections.title: Escalation Pattern
content: Early stage: Minor nitpicking of favors or chores you do for them.
Middle stage: Tying major relationship milestones to arbitrary metrics of your personal improvement that constantly change.
Advanced stage: Total psychological burnout. You realize that literal perfection would not be enough to satisfy them.

sections.title: Why Victims Fall For It
content: The Promise of Completion: The goal seems so tangible. 'If I just lose 10 pounds, he'll love me again.'
The Sunk Cost: You already put in so much effort to reach the first goalpost, you might as well try for the second.
Erosion of confidence: You start believing your 'X' really wasn't good enough, and you deserve the continued punishment.

sections.title: Early Warning Signs
content: No matter what you fix about yourself, they find a new, equally fatal flaw within weeks.
You complete a task they specifically requested, and they immediately find the one tiny mistake in it.
You feel a chronic, background sense of 'not being enough'.

sections.title: Advanced Warning Signs
content: You give up entirely (Learned Helplessness) because you know the game is rigged.
You jump through massive, life-altering hoops (surgery, career changes) solely to appease them, and they still aren't satisfied.
You realize you are chasing a ghost. The 'reward' phase simply doesn't exist.

sections.title: Protection Strategies
content: Recognize the mechanism. Stop running the race. The finish line is on wheels.
Base your self-worth on your own metrics, never on a toxic person's shifting demands.
Realize that their dissatisfaction is a feature of their personality, not a result of your failure.

sections.title: Counter-Moves
content: Fails: Trying harder. Apologizing that your effort wasn't good enough.
Works: Withdrawing effort. Produce the boundary. 'I met the agreement we made. If that is no longer sufficient for you, that is your problem to manage.'
Works: Meta-communication. Call out the game. 'I noticed that every time I fix what you ask, you find something new. I'm stepping off the treadmill now.'

sections.title: Reality Check
sections.content: In healthy relationships, people can negotiate new needs as times change. The difference is that healthy partners celebrate your successes and show gratitude for the effort *before* bringing up a new need.
